# Browser and web security

- Render untrusted values as text through framework bindings. Avoid HTML/DOM escape hatches; if rich HTML is a real requirement, sanitize it with a maintained allowlist sanitizer immediately before the sink.
- Use contextual encoding for HTML, attributes, URLs, JavaScript, and CSS. Encoding for one context is not safe in another.
- Validate dynamic URLs with a strict scheme and destination policy. Reject `javascript:`, dangerous `data:` content, credentials in URLs, and untrusted dynamic imports.
- Treat client-side validation and route/role guards as user experience only. Repeat validation and authorization on the server.
- Protect cookie-authenticated state changes with the framework's anti-CSRF mechanism. Use non-safe HTTP methods, validate tokens server-side, and add origin checks where appropriate; `SameSite` is defense in depth.
- Configure CORS with exact trusted origins and only required methods/headers. Never reflect an arbitrary origin or combine credentialed requests with a wildcard origin.
- For `postMessage`, check the exact expected origin and source window, validate a versioned message schema, and send to an exact target origin rather than `*`.
- Keep secrets and privileged business logic out of browser bundles, source maps, hydration state, public environment variables, storage, and markup. Publishable identifiers are not secrets.
- Prefer HttpOnly cookies for browser session credentials. Do not place long-lived bearer tokens in local storage or expose them to third-party scripts without an explicit threat-model decision.
- Use a restrictive, nonce- or hash-based Content Security Policy compatible with the application. Prefer CSP `frame-ancestors` for framing policy, plus `nosniff`, an intentional referrer policy, and HSTS at the HTTPS edge.
- Avoid inline script, string-to-code APIs, DOM clobbering-prone name lookups, and unsafe recursive merging of untrusted object keys.
- Do not cache authenticated or sensitive responses in shared caches. Set an explicit cache policy and include every representation-changing input in a trusted cache key.
